pack.name: Digital Analytics Property
pack.description: Analytics for a data source organised as metrics and dimensions rather than tables — acquisition mix, engagement quality, conversion drop-off and platform experience, each read by measuring one metric and breaking it down.

categories.name: Content & Media Property
categories.description: A property measured on attention — articles, video, or any surface where reading and returning is the outcome.

categories.name: E-commerce Storefront
categories.description: A property measured on completed purchases, where the conversion journey is the spine of the analysis.

categories.name: Lead Generation Site
categories.description: A property measured on enquiries submitted, where the quality of an enquiry matters more than the count.

base.base_context:
# Analyst Briefing

You are analysing a **metrics-and-dimensions data source**. It holds no tables
and answers no SQL: every question is a selection of metrics to measure,
dimensions to break them down by, and a date range.

## Business Profile

{{PROFILE}}

## What Has Been Established So Far

{{PREVIOUS_CONTEXT}}

## Output Language

Write all narrative text — insight names and descriptions, recommendation
titles, summaries — in {{LANGUAGE}}. Keep technical tokens in English
regardless of that setting: metric and dimension names as the source spells
them, JSON keys, severity values, analysis-area ids and citation markers.
base.exploration:
# Exploration

This source has no tables, no joins and no SQL. A query is a **selection**: one
or more metrics to measure, the dimensions to break them down by, and a date
range. The source computes the result.

Use only names that appear in the catalog below, spelled exactly as it spells
them. An invented name is not a query this source refuses cheaply — it spends
quota and returns nothing.

## Method

Pick a metric. Break it down by one dimension. Find the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown. Break that value down by a second
dimension to see what it is made of. Stop when a step stops telling you
something you did not already know.

Two things follow from the source being a cube rather than a warehouse:

- **Not every pairing is legal.** A metric and a dimension can both exist and
  still not be answerable together. A refused pairing is an answer — record it
  and route around it rather than re-asking it unchanged.
- **Breadth is not coverage.** The number of possible slices is the product of
  two long lists, so a run can take many steps without learning anything.
  Prefer one metric followed three dimensions deep over ten metrics broken down
  once each.

## Source Catalog

{{SCHEMA_INFO}}

## Business Profile

{{PROFILE}}

## Analysis Areas

{{ANALYSIS_AREAS}}

## A Note on Names

Any metric or dimension named in this pack's own text is ordinary English, not
a spelling from any particular source's API. Always take the exact name from
the catalog above.
base.recommendations:
# Recommendations

Turn the discovered insights into actions. State what to change, who it
affects, and what would show the change worked — named as a metric and a
dimension **this source can actually measure**, so the claim is checkable in
the next run rather than only arguable.

Each recommendation cites the insights it rests on through
`related_insight_ids`, so a reader can trace a proposal back to the figures
that produced it. A recommendation no insight supports is a guess; drop it
rather than padding the list.

## Discovered Insights

{{INSIGHTS_DATA}}

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only.

```json
{
  "recommendations": [
    {
      "title": "<what to change>",
      "description": "<why, citing the figures>",
      "priority": "high",
      "related_insight_ids": ["<insight id>"],
      "expected_impact": "<the metric and dimension that would move, and roughly how far>"
    }
  ]
}
```

content_media.exploration_context:
This property publishes content and is measured on attention rather than
transactions. Read engagement depth and returning share as the primary
outcomes; treat arrivals as the input to them, not as the result.

ecommerce_storefront.exploration_context:
This property sells. The conversion journey is the spine of the analysis, and
every other breakdown is worth reporting mainly where it explains a difference
in completion. Revenue-shaped metrics, where the catalog offers them, carry
more weight than arrival counts.

lead_generation.exploration_context:
This property collects enquiries. Volume is a weak signal on its own because a
small number of qualified enquiries beats a large number of unqualified ones,
so prefer completion of the enquiry journey broken down by acquisition channel
over any headline arrival figure.

base.name: Acquisition Mix by Channel
base.description: Where arrivals come from and how the mix is shifting — which channels grew or collapsed, and whether a shift in mix explains a change in a downstream metric.
base.prompt:
# Acquisition Mix by Channel

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** arrivals or sessions. **Break it down by** the channel or source dimension. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
campaign or landing entry point to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

A channel whose share moved several points between the current period and the
one before it. Share matters more than absolute count: total arrivals move for
seasonal reasons that say nothing about the mix.

A channel that grew while a downstream metric fell is the finding worth having.
It usually means the new arrivals are a different kind of visitor, not that the
site got worse — and the recommendation for those two is opposite.

## What good and bad look like

A healthy mix has no single channel above roughly two thirds and no channel
that halves quarter over quarter. A channel that appears from nothing is either
a campaign nobody recorded or a misattribution; both are worth naming.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

```json
{
  "insights": [
    {
      "name": "<short title naming the metric and the slice>",
      "description": "<2-4 sentences citing the exact figures from the query results, including the comparison the slice is out of line with>",
      "severity": "high",
      "affected_count": 0,
      "confidence": 0.0,
      "source_steps": [1, 2],
      "risk_score": 0.0,
      "metrics": { "primary_metric": "<metric as the catalog spells it>", "current_value": 0, "previous_value": 0 },
      "indicators": ["<one human-readable bullet per supporting figure>"],
      "target_segment": "<one sentence of prose describing who is affected — never a filter expression>"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Query Results

{{QUERY_RESULTS}}

base.name: Engagement Quality by Segment
base.description: Whether visits are doing anything — depth, duration and repeat visits, broken down by the segments that plausibly differ, so a headline average is never reported on its own.
base.prompt:
# Engagement Quality by Segment

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** an engagement metric such as engaged sessions or average engagement time. **Break it down by** one audience dimension at a time. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
device or entry point to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

An average that hides two populations. Engagement metrics are the ones most
often reported as a single number and least often true as one: a small,
highly-engaged cohort and a large, bouncing one average to a figure that
describes nobody.

Compare each slice against the property-wide figure rather than against a
target. The target belongs to the business profile; the comparison belongs to
the data.

## What good and bad look like

A slice engaging at half the property-wide rate is worth an insight even when
the property-wide rate is healthy. A slice engaging at twice the rate is worth
one too — it is usually the cohort the business should be acquiring more of.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

```json
{
  "insights": [
    {
      "name": "<short title naming the metric and the slice>",
      "description": "<2-4 sentences citing the exact figures from the query results, including the comparison the slice is out of line with>",
      "severity": "high",
      "affected_count": 0,
      "confidence": 0.0,
      "source_steps": [1, 2],
      "risk_score": 0.0,
      "metrics": { "primary_metric": "<metric as the catalog spells it>", "current_value": 0, "previous_value": 0 },
      "indicators": ["<one human-readable bullet per supporting figure>"],
      "target_segment": "<one sentence of prose describing who is affected — never a filter expression>"
    }
  ]
}
```

base.name: Conversion Drop-off by Step
base.description: Where the intended journey loses people, measured step by step and broken down by the dimension that separates the people who complete it from the people who do not.
base.prompt:
# Conversion Drop-off by Step

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** the conversion or completion metric for each step of the journey. **Break it down by** the step or event-name dimension. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
channel or device to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

The step with the largest fall in completions relative to the step before it,
not the step with the fewest completions. The last step always has the fewest;
that is arithmetic, not a finding.

Then ask whether the fall is the same for everyone. A drop-off concentrated in
one device, one channel or one country is a fixable defect. A drop-off spread
evenly is a design question, and saying which of the two it is is most of the
value of this area.

## What good and bad look like

Step-to-step completion that degrades smoothly is normal. A single step that
loses most of its traffic while its neighbours do not is a defect until proven
otherwise.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

```json
{
  "insights": [
    {
      "name": "<short title naming the metric and the slice>",
      "description": "<2-4 sentences citing the exact figures from the query results, including the comparison the slice is out of line with>",
      "severity": "high",
      "affected_count": 0,
      "confidence": 0.0,
      "source_steps": [1, 2],
      "risk_score": 0.0,
      "metrics": { "primary_metric": "<metric as the catalog spells it>", "current_value": 0, "previous_value": 0 },
      "indicators": ["<one human-readable bullet per supporting figure>"],
      "target_segment": "<one sentence of prose describing who is affected — never a filter expression>"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Query Results

{{QUERY_RESULTS}}

base.name: Audience Composition and Growth
base.description: Who is arriving and how that population is changing — new against returning, and the geographies and languages the property is actually serving as opposed to the ones it was built for.
base.prompt:
# Audience Composition and Growth

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** users or arrivals. **Break it down by** the new-versus-returning dimension. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
country or language to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

A property whose growth is entirely new visitors is not growing, it is
churning. Read the new/returning split first and every other breakdown through
it.

Then look for a geography or language the business profile does not mention.
An audience the property was never built for is either an opportunity or a
misattribution, and the profile is what tells you which.

## What good and bad look like

A returning share that falls for two consecutive periods while total arrivals
rise is the shape of a property buying traffic it cannot keep.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

base.name: Content Performance by Entry Point
base.description: Which entry points carry the property — the pages, screens or campaigns people arrive on, ranked by what happens after the arrival rather than by arrivals alone.
base.prompt:
# Content Performance by Entry Point

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** arrivals and a downstream metric together. **Break it down by** the landing page or entry screen dimension. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
channel to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

Rank entry points by the downstream metric, not by arrivals. The most-visited
entry point is almost always the home page and almost never the finding.

The pairs worth naming are the two off-diagonal ones: high arrivals with poor
downstream performance (spend arriving at something that does not work), and
low arrivals with strong downstream performance (something that works and
nobody can find).

## What good and bad look like

A single entry point above roughly half of all arrivals is a concentration
risk. An entry point with strong arrivals and a downstream metric well below
the property-wide figure is the clearest fixable loss this source can show.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

```json
{
  "insights": [
    {
      "name": "<short title naming the metric and the slice>",
      "description": "<2-4 sentences citing the exact figures from the query results, including the comparison the slice is out of line with>",
      "severity": "high",
      "affected_count": 0,
```

base.name: Platform and Device Experience
base.description: Whether the experience holds up across devices, browsers and platforms — the breakdown most likely to hide a defect that looks like a business problem.
base.prompt:
# Platform and Device Experience

This source is queried by selecting metrics and dimensions over a date
range — there are no tables, no joins and no SQL.

**Measure** an engagement or conversion metric. **Break it down by** the device category or platform dimension. **Find** the value that is out of
line with the rest of the breakdown, then break that value down again by
browser or operating system to see what it is made of.

## What to look for

A metric that is materially worse on one platform than the others. This is the
breakdown where a technical defect shows up as what looks like a commercial
problem, so it is worth running even when nothing else suggests it.

Check the share of arrivals on the affected platform before deciding severity.
A defect on a platform carrying 2% of arrivals is real and low priority; the
same defect on 60% is the property's main problem.

## What good and bad look like

Platforms differing by a few percent is normal. One platform at half the
property-wide figure is a defect, and the insight should say so plainly rather
than describing it as a segment preference.

## Required Output Format

Return JSON only. Every insight names the slice it is about — the metric, the
dimension value, and the period — so a reader can re-run it without guessing.

```json
{
  "insights": [
    {
      "name": "<short title naming the metric and the slice>",
      "description": "<2-4 sentences citing the exact figures from the query results, including the comparison the slice is out of line with>",
      "severity": "high",
      "affected_count": 0,
      "confidence": 0.0,
      "source_steps": [1, 2],
      "risk_score": 0.0,
      "metrics": { "primary_metric": "<metric as the catalog spells it>", "current_value": 0, "previous_value": 0 },
      "indicators": ["<one human-readable bullet per supporting figure>"],
      "target_segment": "<one sentence of prose describing who is affected — never a filter expression>"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Query Results

{{QUERY_RESULTS}}

property_purpose.title: What this property is for
property_purpose.description: One sentence: what the business wants people to do here (read, buy, enquire, sign up).

primary_outcome.title: Primary outcome metric
primary_outcome.description: The metric the business is actually judged on, as the source's catalog spells it.

secondary_outcomes.title: Secondary outcome metrics
secondary_outcomes.description: Metrics that matter but do not decide, in the catalog's spelling.

reporting_period.title: Reporting period
reporting_period.description: The grain the business reviews results at.

comparison_window.title: Comparison window
comparison_window.description: What a period is compared against — the previous period, the same period last year, or a fixed baseline.

seasonality.title: Seasonality drivers
seasonality.description: Recurring events that move the numbers for reasons unrelated to performance (term dates, sales periods, campaign flights).

acquisition_channels.title: Channels the business actually buys
acquisition_channels.description: Named so an unexpected channel in the data can be told from a known one.

key_journeys.title: Journeys that matter
key_journeys.description: The step sequences the business cares about completing, named in its own words.

audience_markets.title: Markets served
audience_markets.description: Countries or regions the property is built for, so an unserved market showing up is recognisable.

platform_priorities.title: Platforms that matter most
platform_priorities.description: Where the business expects its audience to be, so a platform defect can be weighted.

known_gaps.title: Known measurement gaps
known_gaps.description: Anything the business already knows is untracked or mis-tracked, so the analysis does not report it as a finding.

excluded_traffic.title: Traffic to discount
excluded_traffic.description: Internal, test or bot traffic the business knows about but the source may still count.
